svg.aria-label: The codex from the 1530s to now
svg.text: The codex, from the paper to the present
Five centuries above, the last sixty years below. Above each line, the book; below it, the people who tried to read it.

g.data-desc: The paper the codex is written on is reported to be Venetian, made in the 1530s. The watermark study is cited at second hand and this edition has not seen it.

On Kiraly and Tokai's reading, one of the last leaves counts one thousand five hundred and sixty years from the Ascension, giving 1593. That summer the Long Turkish War began. Where in Hungary the codex was written, and by whom, is not known.
A 1743 catalogue of the Batthyany library at Rohonc lists 'Magyar imadsagok, volumen I in 12' -- Hungarian prayers, one small volume. It may or may not be the codex.

Count Gusztav Batthyany gives his library at Rohonc, some 30,000 volumes, to the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. The codex is in it and takes the town's name. Most accounts say 1838; the Hungarian article on the town says 1839.
Burgenland passes from Hungary to Austria. Rechnitz, an older German name for the town, is again official; its Hungarian name remains Rohonc. The codex itself stays in Budapest.
Ferenc Toldy is the first scholar to study it. Pal Hunfalvy follows; neither reads a word.
Karoly Szabo proposes that the codex is a hoax by Samuel Literati Nemes, a known forger of antiquities. The charge stands in the literature for a century and a half.
Josef and Konstantin Jirecek, then Bernhard Julg at Innsbruck, examine it and find nothing they can read.
Kalman Nemati counts the distinct signs and finds 792 -- far too many for an alphabet, which is the first real fact about the script.
An anonymous author publishes a free, glyph-by-glyph transcription of the whole codex, in an alphabet of their own. It is the independent check this edition's tests lean on.
All 441 written pages rendered into English end to end, every word marked for how well it is known, with the tests and the data published beside it.

g.data-label: Gyurk: right to left, and numbers
g.data-desc: Otto Gyurk shows the writing runs right to left and finds the numbers. His observation that the repeated sequences break at the line is the one this edition's whole reading rests on.
g.text: Gyurk: right to left, and numbers

g.data-desc: Miklos Locsmandi runs the text through a computer and rejects the idea that it is meaningless filler.
Attila Nyiri reads it as Sumerian ligatures. Dismissed at once.
Viorica Enachiuc publishes a reading as a Daco-Romanian dialect of Vulgar Latin, a history of the Vlachs in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, read right to left and bottom to top. Rejected.
Mahesh Kumar Singh reads it as a variant of Brahmi carrying an apocryphal gospel, left to right. Rejected.

g.data-label: Lang: a cipher, not a hoax
g.data-desc: Benedek Lang argues the codex is a consciously encoded text and not a forgery, and writes the history of the problem (A Rohonci kod, 2011; in English as The Rohonc Code, 2021).
g.text: Lang: a cipher, not a hoax

g.data-desc: Gabor Tokai identifies the codes for the evangelists and reads the year numbers as Anno Mundi; Levente Zoltan Kiraly works out the chapter structure and a table of contents.

Cracking the code of the Rohonc Codex, in Cryptologia: a code system rather than a cipher, 841 dictionary codes glossed in this edition's merged data, the proposed date 1593, and the content a Catholic reader of its time. The dictionary this edition stands on.
Kiraly's paper on the theological character of the codex, with the transcription and dictionary put online at rechnitzer-kodex.hu so the claims can be checked.

svg.text: the turns the story hangs on
